Activity Description: Wireframing is sketching the bare-bones layout of a screen, showing where things go without color or polish. It is about structure, not looks.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Starting rough lets the team test and change ideas cheaply before anyone builds a finished-looking design.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens during the Implement work and produces wireframes that grow into prototypes. Teams often wireframe together in a workshop so everyone shapes the layout.
How To Complete the Activity: Start from the user's task and block out where each piece goes on the screen. Use a tool like Figma or FigJam to lay out simple boxes, then share it for quick feedback.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Release scope definition is deciding what will and will not go into an upcoming release. It draws a clear line around the next chunk of work.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A focused release actually ships, and clear scope sets honest expectations with everyone involved.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It spans discovery through launch and produces epics, release-level scope, and the release plan. Teams often scope together so priorities are shared, and re-scope as they learn.
How To Complete the Activity: List the possible work, then sort it into what is in and what waits. In Notion or FigJam, agree on the cut with the team and write down what the release will include.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Requirements gathering is collecting what a product needs to do by talking to stakeholders and users. It turns scattered wants into a clear list.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Getting requirements right early is one of the biggest reasons projects succeed instead of drifting.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and feeds problem statements, acceptance criteria, and user stories. It is often a workshop so the whole room agrees.
How To Complete the Activity: Ask lots of open questions and listen for the real need behind each request. Capture what you hear in Notion or Trello and play it back to confirm you got it right.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Requirements refinement is sharpening rough requirements into clear, buildable detail. It is the tidy-up that makes a to-do list ready to work from.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Refined requirements mean the team stops guessing what an item really means, so building goes smoothly.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens across discovery and requirements and produces acceptance criteria, user stories, and a refined backlog. Teams often refine together in a quick working session.
How To Complete the Activity: Take each rough item and add detail, examples, and a clear definition of done. In Notion or Trello, resize and reword items with the team until they are clear.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Design component creation is building the reusable interface pieces, like buttons and cards, that a product is assembled from. It is making the parts once so they can be used everywhere.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Reusable components speed up design and keep a product looking consistent instead of slightly different on every screen.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and builds the component library that feeds the design system. It supports every screen the team designs.
How To Complete the Activity: Identify the pieces used again and again, then build each one cleanly in Figma. Set them up as shared components so the whole team can reuse them.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Brand identity formation is shaping how a product looks, sounds, and feels so it is recognizable and consistent. It gives the product a personality.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear identity builds trust and makes a product memorable, tying the whole experience together.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces the editorial style guide, brand identity, archetypes, and brand assets. It is often shaped in a collaborative workshop.
How To Complete the Activity: Explore words and visuals that capture the product's character, then agree on a direction. Use Figma and Notion to define the voice, colors, and rules others will follow.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Writing requirements is putting down clearly what needs to be built and how you will know it is done. It captures needs in a form the team can act on.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Written, agreed requirements keep designers and developers building the same thing instead of different versions.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It spans requirements and launch and produces acceptance criteria, user stories, task flows, and scope. Teams often draft these together to align quickly.
How To Complete the Activity: Write each need as a short, testable statement with clear acceptance criteria. In Notion or Trello, review them with the team and adjust anything unclear.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Icon and logo creation is designing the small, recognizable marks that represent a brand or an action. These tiny visuals carry a lot of meaning.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear, consistent icons and logos make a product easier to use and instantly recognizable.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces logo and brand assets. It builds on the brand identity the team has set.
How To Complete the Activity: Sketch several directions, then refine the strongest in Figma. Test them small to be sure they stay clear and simple at real size.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Feature vision definition is deciding what a specific feature should achieve and why it matters. It sets the point of a feature before the details.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear feature vision keeps the team building toward a purpose instead of just adding functionality.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Requirements work and shapes the acceptance criteria that define the feature. It is often set with the team so everyone shares the goal.
How To Complete the Activity: Describe the problem the feature solves and what success looks like. In Notion or FigJam, agree on the vision with the team before detailing it.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Feature scope definition is deciding what is included in a single feature and what is left out. It draws the boundary around one piece of work.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear boundaries keep a feature from ballooning and help the team estimate and finish it reliably.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Requirements work and feeds the acceptance criteria for the feature. Teams often scope features together to keep priorities shared.
How To Complete the Activity: List everything the feature could do, then agree on the must-haves for now. Capture the decision in Notion or Trello so it is clear later.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Generating problem statements is writing short, clear descriptions of the problems worth solving, from the user's point of view. It names the real issue plainly.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Clear problems keep the team from building slick solutions to the wrong thing.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and produces problem statements, checklists, and how-might-we questions. It is often done as a group so problems are shared.
How To Complete the Activity: Turn what you learned from users into simple 'who struggles with what and why' statements. In FigJam or Notion, refine them with the team until they ring true.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Analyzing research findings is making sense of what a study turned up to find what it really means. It is where raw notes become insight.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Careful analysis keeps the team from jumping to conclusions, so decisions rest on what the data actually shows.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and acceptance testing and produces research reports, rainbow tables, and analysis. Teams often analyze together to catch more patterns.
How To Complete the Activity: Group your notes into themes and look for what repeats. Use FigJam, Dovetail, or a spreadsheet to cluster findings and write down the clear takeaways.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Strategy definition is deciding how a product or team will reach its goals. It sets the approach before the doing begins.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear strategy focuses effort on what will actually move things forward instead of scattering energy.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery work and feeds the business plan and go-to-market plan. It is often shaped with the team in a working session.
How To Complete the Activity: Clarify the goal, then map a few realistic paths to it and pick one. In Notion or FigJam, write the approach down so the whole team can follow it.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Sprint planning is the team agreeing on what they will complete in the next short work cycle. It picks a focused slice of the backlog.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear, achievable target keeps agile work steady and lets the team make smart trade-offs.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and repeats every sprint, producing the sprint plan and goals. It is a team workshop by design.
How To Complete the Activity: Review the top of the backlog, estimate what fits, and agree on a goal. In Notion or Trello, commit to the sprint's work together.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Level of effort estimation is the team's best guess at how much work an item will take. It sizes the work so it can be planned.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Estimates help the team plan realistically and avoid over-committing a sprint.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across discovery, requirements, and every sprint, refining the backlog and sprint goals. Teams estimate together so many views are heard.
How To Complete the Activity: Compare each item to ones you have done before and agree on a rough size. Capture the estimates in Notion or Trello for planning.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Velocity calculation measures how much work a team actually completes per sprint. It turns past sprints into a planning guide.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Knowing real velocity helps a team plan future sprints honestly instead of hopefully.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and across sprints, informing the sprint plan and goals. It supports the scrum master's planning.
How To Complete the Activity: Add up the work finished in recent sprints to find an average. Track it in Notion or a spreadsheet and use it to size the next sprint.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Identifying priorities is deciding which work matters most right now. It sorts a big pile into a clear order.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear order means effort goes to what matters most instead of what is nearest or loudest.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and requirements and shapes the prioritized and refined backlog. Teams often prioritize together to align.
How To Complete the Activity: Weigh each item by value and effort, then rank them. In FigJam, agree on the order with the team and record it.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Presenting research results is sharing what a study found with the team in a clear, usable way. It turns insight into shared understanding.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Research only helps if the team acts on it, and a clear share makes that far more likely.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and produces research reports and usability test reports. It is often a presentation or workshop for the team.
How To Complete the Activity: Lead with the key findings and what they mean for the work. Use Notion or presentation tools to tell a simple, honest story.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Kickoff, or intake, is the first working session where the team and client get aligned before the work begins. It sets the tone for everything after.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Projects that start fuzzy tend to stay fuzzy, so a clear kickoff prevents confusion down the road.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It opens a project or phase and produces the statement of work, project plan, goals, and KPIs. It can recur when direction shifts, and it is a shared workshop.
How To Complete the Activity: Talk through goals, scope, roles, and how you will work together. Capture agreements in Notion so everyone can refer back to them.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Roles: Scrum Master, Project Management, Product Operations
Activity Description: Defining team working agreements is setting the ground rules for how a team will work together. The team writes its own social contract.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Agreed norms head off friction, so the team spends energy on the work instead of avoidable conflict.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and produces working agreements and a psychological safety plan. It is a group workshop by nature.
How To Complete the Activity: Discuss how you want to communicate, meet, and handle disagreement, then agree on a few clear norms. Write them in Notion where everyone can see them.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

Activity Description: This is clarifying who owns what on a team. It makes sure every important job has a clear owner.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It prevents both the 'someone else has it' gap and two people redoing the same work.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens at intake and produces the RACI chart. It is best done together so roles are truly agreed.
How To Complete the Activity: Map each key responsibility to who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed. Capture it in a RACI chart in Notion or FigJam.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

Activity Description: Moderating UX research is guiding a research session live, like an interview or usability test, keeping it on track. The moderator draws out honest, useful input.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A well-run session gets real insight instead of polite or leading answers.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and acceptance testing and feeds research reports and analysis. It is often observed by teammates for shared learning.
How To Complete the Activity: Prepare a light guide, then ask open questions and listen more than you talk. Run remote sessions over Zoom and take careful notes.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Secondary research is learning from what others have already published, rather than gathering new data yourself. It is standing on existing knowledge.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It is a fast, cheap way to get grounded before investing in new studies.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs through discovery and acceptance testing and feeds journey maps, research reports, and analysis. It often kicks off a research effort.
How To Complete the Activity: Gather trustworthy sources and pull out what is relevant to your questions. Organize the findings in FigJam or a spreadsheet.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Card sorting asks people to group and label items the way that makes sense to them. It reveals how users naturally organize information.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It helps a team structure a product to match how users think, not how the team happens to.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It feeds research plans and analysis and shapes information architecture like sitemaps. It can run as a group activity or a remote study.
How To Complete the Activity: Give participants items to sort into groups they name. Run it in Optimal Workshop or UXtweak, then look for common patterns.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Interviewing is talking one-on-one with users to understand their needs, goals, and frustrations. It is the most direct way to learn from people.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Nothing beats hearing directly from users for understanding what they actually need.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and feeds the research report. Teammates often observe to build shared understanding.
How To Complete the Activity: Prepare open questions, then listen closely and follow curiosity. Run remote interviews on Zoom and record with permission.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Surveys collect answers from many people through a set of questions. They trade depth for reach.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Surveys show how common a need or opinion is across a larger group.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: They run in discovery and acceptance testing and feed research reports, plans, and analysis. They pair well with interviews for depth plus breadth.
How To Complete the Activity: Write clear, unbiased questions and keep it short. Use a survey tool, then analyze the results in a spreadsheet.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Storyboarding tells the story of a user's experience as a series of simple frames, like a comic strip. It shows the experience in real-life context.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It helps a team imagine the situation around a product, not just the screens, sparking more human ideas.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and produces the storyboard, building on personas and journey maps. It is often sketched together.
How To Complete the Activity: Draw the key moments of a user's story, frame by frame. Use Figma or FigJam and keep the sketches rough and quick.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Product positioning is deciding how a product presents itself and stands out from alternatives. It shapes the story customers hear.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clear position helps everyone tell a consistent story and helps customers see why the product is for them.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across discovery, vision, and launch and feeds positioning statements, the value proposition, and marketing. It is often shaped with the team.
How To Complete the Activity: Define who the product is for and why it is different, in a sentence or two. Refine it in Notion with the team until it is sharp.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: A diary study asks people to log their experiences over days or weeks. It captures real life as it unfolds, not just a snapshot.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It reveals patterns and moments that a single session would miss.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and feeds the research report. It complements interviews with over-time insight.
How To Complete the Activity: Ask participants to record entries at set moments, then review for patterns. Collect entries in FigJam or a spreadsheet.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: A contextual inquiry is observing and talking with users in their real environment while they work. It studies people where things actually happen.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Seeing real context reveals needs and workarounds people would never think to mention.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and feeds the research report. Teammates often observe to learn firsthand.
How To Complete the Activity: Watch users in their setting and ask about what they do as they do it. Take notes in Notion or FigJam, or record over Zoom.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Ethnographic observation is watching how people behave in their natural setting, with minimal interference. You learn by seeing, not just asking.
Why Is This Activity Important?: People often do things differently from how they describe them, and observation catches that gap.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs in discovery and acceptance testing and feeds research reports, plans, and analysis.
How To Complete the Activity: Spend time watching real behavior and note what surprises you. Capture observations in Notion or a spreadsheet.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Usability testing watches real people try to use a design to see where they succeed and struggle. It puts the design to the test with actual users.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It gives hard evidence about what works, so fixes target real problems, not guesses.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs in discovery and acceptance testing and feeds usability test reports, research reports, and analysis. It often loops right back into design.
How To Complete the Activity: Give people real tasks and watch without helping, then note where they get stuck. Run sessions on Zoom or Maze and summarize the findings.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Prototype concept testing puts an early prototype in front of users to check whether an idea works before building it. It tests the concept, not the polish.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Testing early saves the team from building something users do not actually want.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It feeds research reports, plans, and analysis and loops back into design. It is a core agile habit of learning before committing.
How To Complete the Activity: Show the prototype, give a task, and watch the reaction. Use Maze or Zoom, then feed what you learn back into the design.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: A/B prototype test creation builds two versions of a design so you can compare which works better. It sets up a head-to-head test.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Comparing real options with users settles debates with evidence instead of opinion.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces the prototypes being tested. It supports usability and concept testing.
How To Complete the Activity: Make two clear variations that differ in one meaningful way. Build them in Figma and set them up for testing in Maze or Dovetail.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: UI kit creation is building the shared set of interface styles and elements a product uses. It is the toolbox designers pull from.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A shared kit keeps a product consistent and speeds up design work.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces the design system and component library.
How To Complete the Activity: Define the core styles and elements, then build them cleanly as reusable pieces in Figma so the team can share them.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Developing information architecture is organizing a product's content and structure so people can find things. It is the blueprint for how a product is arranged.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Good structure is the difference between a product that feels obvious and one where people get lost.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces prototypes, sitemaps, and taxonomy.
How To Complete the Activity: Map the content into logical groups and a clear hierarchy. Sketch the structure in Figma or FigJam and test it with users.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Prototype creation is building an interactive version of a design that people can click through. It makes an idea feel real before it is built.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A prototype lets the team test a real experience early and cheaply.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces wireframes and prototypes at different levels of polish.
How To Complete the Activity: Turn your designs into clickable screens in Figma. Keep it just real enough to test the questions you care about.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Tracking milestone progress is keeping an eye on how the project is moving against its goals. It is the regular pulse-check on the work.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It helps a team spot slippage early and adjust before small delays become big ones.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens across the project and feeds the Gantt chart and roadmap. It supports steady, visible agile delivery.
How To Complete the Activity: Check what is done against the plan and note what is at risk. Update the roadmap in Notion so everyone can see where things stand.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Tracking epic progress is following how a large body of work is advancing toward completion. It keeps big efforts from stalling unseen.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It gives the team and stakeholders a clear view of progress on the things that matter most.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Vision work and feeds the roadmap. It supports product ownership.
How To Complete the Activity: Break the epic into visible pieces and mark progress as they finish. Track it in Notion or Trello.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: A UX heuristics analysis reviews a design against well-known usability rules to catch obvious problems. It is an expert gut-check for the experience.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It quickly surfaces common issues without needing a full study.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in requirements and implement and feeds the UX audit report.
How To Complete the Activity: Walk through the product against a checklist of usability principles, noting each violation. Record findings in FigJam or a spreadsheet.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Activity Description: Product roadmap maintenance is keeping the roadmap current as plans and priorities change. A roadmap only helps if it stays honest.
Why Is This Activity Important?: An up-to-date roadmap keeps everyone aligned and expectations realistic.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Vision work and keeps the roadmap accurate. It is revisited often as the team learns.
How To Complete the Activity: Review the roadmap regularly, adjust for what changed, and communicate updates. Keep it in Notion or Trello.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Market research is learning about the market, customers, and competitors a product operates in. It reads the landscape a product enters.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It grounds big decisions in evidence about real demand rather than hunches.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across discovery, vision, and launch and feeds the business plan, positioning, and go-to-market work.
How To Complete the Activity: Gather data on customers and competitors and pull out the patterns. Organize findings in Notion for the team.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian's guide to product management: https://www.atlassian.com/agile/product-management

Activity Description: Scheduling meetings is lining up the right people at the right time to move work forward. It sounds simple but keeps a team in sync.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Well-run, well-timed meetings keep everyone aligned without wasting people's time.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens across the project and produces meeting agendas. It supports project management.
How To Complete the Activity: Find a time that works, set a clear agenda, and invite only who is needed. Use Notion and Zoom to organize and host.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: QA testing is checking that a product works as intended before it reaches users. It is the safety net that catches bugs.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Shipping something broken costs far more than catching it early, in money and trust.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in launch and acceptance testing and produces the QA test plan, cases, and analysis. In agile work it happens continuously, not just at the end.
How To Complete the Activity: Run through the test cases and log anything that fails. Track issues in Notion or a spreadsheet and confirm fixes.
Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

Activity Description: Autotest creation is writing tests that a computer runs automatically to check a product. It lets the same checks run over and over without manual effort.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Automated tests catch problems fast every time code changes, which keeps quality steady.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in launch and produces QA test cases. It supports ongoing quality as the product grows.
How To Complete the Activity: Identify the checks worth automating, then write tests that run them. Manage them in Notion and your code tools.
Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

Activity Description: Tracking sprint progress is watching how a sprint is going day to day. It keeps the current cycle honest.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A daily read on progress lets the team adjust before the sprint runs out.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across sprints and feeds the burn down chart, refined backlog, and sprint plan.
How To Complete the Activity: Check what is done and what is stuck each day. Update the board in Notion or Trello and raise blockers early.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: User acceptance testing checks whether the finished work actually meets users' and stakeholders' needs. It is the final does-this-really-work check.
Why Is This Activity Important?: It confirms the product does what people need before it goes live, protecting against costly misses.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It runs across discovery, implement, launch, and acceptance testing and feeds research reports and stakeholder feedback.
How To Complete the Activity: Have real users try the work against the agreed criteria and note gaps. Capture results in Notion or Trello.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Roles: Product Ownership, UX (User Experience) Design, UX (User Experience) Research, UX (User Experience) Writing
Activity Description: Facilitating agile workshops is guiding a group session so the team collaborates well and reaches a clear outcome. The facilitator holds the space, not the answers.
Why Is This Activity Important?: Well-run workshops turn a room of individuals into shared thinking and real decisions.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in discovery and implement and supports many deliverables. Workshops are where a lot of agile collaboration happens.
How To Complete the Activity: Plan a clear goal and a few activities, then guide the group and keep everyone involved. Run it in FigJam or over Zoom.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Activity Description: Clickable prototype creation is making a design you can actually click through, so it behaves like a real product. It brings a static design to life.
Why Is This Activity Important?: A clickable version lets people experience a flow and gives far better feedback than a picture.
How Does the Activity Relate to Mileston: It happens in the Implement work and produces prototypes at different levels of polish.
How To Complete the Activity: Link your screens so taps lead somewhere in Figma. Add just enough interaction to test the flow.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/
